items.title: Integration of the Princely States (1947–49)
items.body:
### How 565 states became one country

**In one line:** When the British left, India was not one country but British India plus hundreds of self-ruling princely states; Sardar Patel persuaded almost all of them to join the Union.

**Why it is asked:** This is a favourite for statement-based and assertion-reason questions, especially the three 'hard cases' (Junagadh, Hyderabad, Kashmir) and the exact instruments used.

**The story**

- In 1947 India was **British India plus about 565 princely states**. When British **paramountcy** (overlordship) lapsed, each state could legally, under the **Indian Independence Act**, **join India, join Pakistan, or remain independent** — a real risk of the map breaking into pieces. **Don't confuse** the ~565 princely states were *outside* British India (ruled by their own princes under British paramountcy); British India itself was the directly ruled provinces.
- **Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel** (Deputy Prime Minister and Home Minister), helped by the civil servant **V.P. Menon**, ran a new **States Department** and persuaded the vast majority to join India by August 1947.

**The instruments used:**

- **Instrument of Accession** — a legal document by which a state joined India, at first handing over only **three subjects: defence, external affairs and communications**.
- **Standstill Agreement** — kept existing arrangements running while accession was negotiated.

**Picture it — the three hard cases**

| State | Problem | Resolution |
|---|---|---|
| Junagadh | Hindu-majority; Nawab acceded to Pakistan | Plebiscite, Feb 1948, favoured India |
| Hyderabad | Nizam wanted independence; Razakars militia | Operation Polo, Sept 1948 (Police Action) |
| Jammu & Kashmir | Maharaja Hari Singh initially wished to remain independent and signed a Standstill Agreement (with Pakistan) | Instrument of Accession, 26 Oct 1947 after a tribal invasion; Article 370 |

So the **Instrument of Accession alone was not always sufficient**: these three states required a plebiscite, military action or accession under invasion before their integration was settled.

**Terms explained**

- **Paramountcy:** the supremacy the British Crown held over the princely states; it simply ended (lapsed) at independence rather than passing to India or Pakistan.
- **Plebiscite:** a direct vote by the people to decide a question (here, which country to join).
- **Razakars:** a private militia in Hyderabad, led by **Kasim Razvi** of the Ittehad-ul-Muslimeen, that backed the Nizam's refusal to join India.
- **Article 370:** a provision that gave Jammu & Kashmir special status (effectively abrogated in 2019).

**Don't confuse:** **Operation Polo = Hyderabad** (not Junagadh). **Junagadh = plebiscite**; **Kashmir = accession amid invasion**. The Instrument of Accession first ceded only three subjects, not full control.

**Remember it:** the three hard cases are 'J-H-K' = **Junagadh (plebiscite), Hyderabad (Operation Polo), Kashmir (Article 370)**. Patel's success earned him the title **'Iron Man of India'**.

**TL;DR**

- India in 1947 = British India + about 565 princely states; each could join India, join Pakistan or stay independent.
- Patel, aided by V.P. Menon and the States Department, integrated most of them.
- The Instrument of Accession first ceded only defence, external affairs and communications.
- Junagadh (plebiscite Feb 1948); Hyderabad (Operation Polo, Sept 1948); J&K (accession 26 Oct 1947, Article 370).
keyPoints: India in 1947 = British India + about 565 princely states, each free to join India, join Pakistan or stay independent.
Sardar Patel, aided by V.P. Menon and the States Department, integrated most princely states.
The Instrument of Accession transferred only defence, external affairs and communications to the Union.
Junagadh joined India via a February 1948 plebiscite after its Nawab acceded to Pakistan.
Hyderabad was integrated by Operation Polo (Sept 1948) against the Nizam and the Razakars.
Jammu & Kashmir acceded on 26 October 1947 (Instrument of Accession) amid a tribal invasion; Article 370 gave special status.
items.mnemonic: Three hard cases 'J-H-K' = Junagadh (plebiscite), Hyderabad (Operation Polo), Kashmir (Article 370).

items.title: Commissions on States Reorganisation
items.body:
### The committees that redrew the map

**In one line:** After 1947 India's internal boundaries were a messy patchwork, so three bodies in turn studied whether to redraw states by language.

**Why it is asked:** The three bodies and their differing stands are a classic match-the-following; the trap is mixing up who rejected language and who accepted it.

**The story**

- In 1950 the states were sorted into four classes: **Part A** (former governors' provinces), **Part B** (former princely states, each under a *Rajpramukh*), **Part C** (chief commissioners' provinces) and **Part D** (only the Andaman & Nicobar Islands).
- The loudest demand — strongest in the **South** — was to redraw boundaries on a **linguistic** (language) basis, so three bodies examined the idea one after another.

**Picture it — the three bodies**

| Body | Year | Position |
|---|---|---|
| Dhar Commission | 1948 | Rejected language as the basis; stressed administrative convenience |
| JVP Committee | 1948 | Nehru, Patel, Pattabhi Sitaramayya; advised delaying linguistic states but noted public sentiment |
| Fazl Ali Commission (SRC) | 1953 | Accepted language as a factor but rejected 'one language–one state'; proposed 16 states, 3 UTs |

- The **Fazl Ali Commission** (with K.M. Panikkar and H.N. Kunzru) became the basis of the **States Reorganisation Act, 1956**.

**Terms explained**

- **Rajpramukh:** the title given to the head (usually a former ruler) of a Part B state, like a governor.
- **Linguistic basis:** drawing a state's borders so that people who speak the same language live in the same state.
- **SRC:** States Reorganisation Commission, the formal name of the Fazl Ali Commission.
- **'One language–one state':** the idea that every language should get exactly one state of its own — which the SRC rejected (e.g. Hindi is spoken across several states).

**Don't confuse:** **Dhar (1948) said NO** to language; **JVP (1948) said WAIT**; **Fazl Ali (1953) said YES, with limits**. The JVP Committee's 'J-V-P' stands for **Jawaharlal (Nehru), Vallabhbhai (Patel), Pattabhi (Sitaramayya)**.

**Remember it:** order of bodies 'D-J-F' = **Dhar (no) → JVP (wait) → Fazl Ali (yes, with limits)**.

**TL;DR**

- In 1950 states were Part A (9), Part B (9, princely states under a Rajpramukh), Part C (10) and Part D (Andaman & Nicobar).
- Dhar Commission (1948) rejected language as the primary basis.
- JVP Committee (1948) — Nehru, Patel, Pattabhi Sitaramayya — advised delaying linguistic states.
- Fazl Ali Commission (1953) accepted language as a factor but rejected 'one language–one state'.
- It recommended 16 states and 3 Union Territories and became the basis of the SRA 1956.
keyPoints: In 1950 states were classed as Part A (9), Part B (9, princely states under a Rajpramukh), Part C (10) and Part D (Andaman & Nicobar).
Dhar Commission (1948) rejected language as the primary basis for reorganisation.
JVP Committee (1948) — Nehru, Patel, Pattabhi Sitaramayya — advised delaying linguistic states.
Fazl Ali Commission (1953) accepted language as a factor but rejected 'one language–one state'.
The Fazl Ali Commission recommended 16 states and 3 Union Territories and became the basis of the SRA 1956.
items.mnemonic: Order of bodies 'D-J-F' = Dhar (no) -> JVP (wait) -> Fazl Ali (yes, with limits).

items.title: Andhra State & Linguistic Reorganisation (1953–1956)
items.body:
### How language redrew India's states

**In one line:** Andhra became the first state carved out purely on language in 1953, and its creation forced a nationwide reorganisation in 1956.

**Why it is asked:** This is the direct AP link in the topic; the 1953 (Andhra State) versus 1956 (Andhra Pradesh) dates and the SRA figures are heavily tested.

**The story**

- Telugu-speaking leaders wanted a separate province carved out of the **Madras Presidency**.
- **Potti Sreeramulu's fast-unto-death** — he **died on 15 December 1952** — triggered mass agitation that forced the government's hand.
- **Andhra State was created on 1 October 1953**, the **first state formed on a linguistic basis**, with **Kurnool** as its first capital. This landmark set off similar demands across India.

**The States Reorganisation Act, 1956:**

- Based on the **Fazl Ali Commission**, it reorganised India into **14 states and 6 Union Territories** and scrapped the old Part A/B/C/D scheme.
- It was enacted together with the **7th Constitutional Amendment, 1956**.
- **Andhra Pradesh** was formed on **1 November 1956** by merging Andhra State with the Telugu-speaking areas of Hyderabad State.

**Picture it — later milestones**

| State / event | Year |
|---|---|
| Maharashtra & Gujarat (from Bombay) | 1960 |
| Punjab & Haryana | 1966 |
| Goa liberated (Operation Vijay); statehood 1987 | 1961 |
| Telangana (29th state) | 2014 |
| J&K and Ladakh made Union Territories | 2019 |

**Terms explained**

- **Fast-unto-death:** refusing all food until a demand is met, risking death; a powerful non-violent pressure tactic.
- **Union Territory (UT):** an area administered directly by the central government, not a full state.
- **7th Constitutional Amendment:** the 1956 amendment that gave legal effect to the reorganisation.

**Don't confuse:** **1953 = Andhra State** (capital Kurnool, first linguistic state); **1956 = Andhra Pradesh** (merger with Hyderabad's Telugu areas). The SRC proposed **16 states**, but the Act of 1956 actually created **14 states**.

**Remember it:** Andhra dates — **1953 (Andhra State, Kurnool) → 1956 (Andhra Pradesh, Hyderabad)**.

**TL;DR**

- Potti Sreeramulu's fast-unto-death (died 15 Dec 1952) led to Andhra State on 1 October 1953 — the first linguistic state.
- Kurnool was the first capital of Andhra State.
- The States Reorganisation Act, 1956 created 14 states and 6 Union Territories and abolished the Part A/B/C/D scheme.
- The SRA 1956 was enacted with the 7th Constitutional Amendment.
- Andhra Pradesh was formed on 1 November 1956 by merging Andhra State with Telugu areas of Hyderabad State.
- Goa was liberated via Operation Vijay in 1961 and became a state in 1987.
keyPoints: Potti Sreeramulu's fast-unto-death (died 15 Dec 1952) led to Andhra State on 1 October 1953 — the first linguistic state.
Kurnool was the first capital of Andhra State.
The States Reorganisation Act, 1956 created 14 states and 6 Union Territories and abolished the Part A/B/C/D scheme.
The SRA 1956 was enacted with the 7th Constitutional Amendment.
Andhra Pradesh was formed on 1 November 1956 by merging Andhra State with Telugu areas of Hyderabad State.
Goa was liberated via Operation Vijay in 1961 and became a state in 1987.
items.mnemonic: Andhra dates: 1953 (Andhra State, Kurnool) -> 1956 (Andhra Pradesh, Hyderabad).

items.title: Partition, Rehabilitation & the Republic
items.body:
### Freedom with a wound, then a Republic

**In one line:** Independence in 1947 came with a bloody Partition and a refugee crisis; within three years India turned itself into a democratic Republic.

**Why it is asked:** The two dates (15 Aug 1947 vs 26 Jan 1950) and the first office-holders are standard traps, often tested as a 'which statement is wrong' question.

**The story**

- Independence on **15 August 1947** came with the **Partition** of the subcontinent into India and Pakistan along religious lines.
- Partition caused one of history's **largest mass migrations** (an estimated 10–15 million people displaced) and terrible communal violence; a **Ministry of Rehabilitation** was created to resettle refugees.
- Dividing the army, finances and assets strained both new countries, and **Jammu & Kashmir** became a lasting flashpoint between them.

**Building the Republic:**

- India's **Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950**, making it a **sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic** with **universal adult suffrage** (every adult can vote) and a parliamentary, federal system.
- **Jawaharlal Nehru** was the first **Prime Minister**; **Dr. Rajendra Prasad** was the first **President**.
- The first Council of Ministers included **Patel** (Home & States), **Ambedkar** (Law), **Maulana Azad** (Education) and **R.K. Shanmukham Chetty** (Finance).

**Terms explained**

- **Partition:** the 1947 division of British India into two independent states, India and Pakistan.
- **Universal adult suffrage:** the right of every adult citizen to vote, regardless of wealth, gender or education.
- **Secular:** the state has no official religion and treats all religions equally.

**Don't confuse:** **15 Aug 1947 = Independence/Partition**; **26 Jan 1950 = Republic (Constitution in force)**. On 26 Jan 1950, **Nehru was PM** and **Rajendra Prasad President** — do not swap these roles.

**Remember it:** two dates — **15 Aug 1947 (Independence/Partition) → 26 Jan 1950 (Republic)**.

**TL;DR**

- India became independent on 15 August 1947 amid the Partition into India and Pakistan.
- Partition caused one of the largest mass migrations in history and mass communal violence; a Ministry of Rehabilitation resettled refugees.
- India adopted its Constitution on 26 January 1950 as a sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic with universal adult suffrage.
- Nehru was the first Prime Minister; Dr. Rajendra Prasad was the first President.
- Jammu & Kashmir became a lasting India–Pakistan flashpoint after Partition.
keyPoints: India became independent on 15 August 1947 amid the Partition into India and Pakistan.
Partition caused one of the largest mass migrations in history and mass communal violence; a Ministry of Rehabilitation resettled refugees.
India adopted its Constitution on 26 January 1950 as a sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic with universal adult suffrage.
Nehru was the first Prime Minister; Dr. Rajendra Prasad was the first President.
Jammu & Kashmir became a lasting India–Pakistan flashpoint after Partition.

items.title: Early Nation-Building Milestones & Later Reorganisation (PYQ set)
items.body:
### The dates examiners love to shuffle

**In one line:** A handful of 1950s–70s milestones (nationalisations, the first Communist state government, later state formations) are tested as chronology and single-fact questions.

**Why it is asked:** Chronology ('arrange in order') and one-fact questions are easy marks if the exact years are fixed in memory.

**Picture it — institutional milestones**

| Milestone | Year |
|---|---|
| Air India nationalised | 1953 |
| Imperial Bank of India became State Bank of India (SBI) | 1955 |
| First elected Communist State government (Kerala, E.M.S. Namboodiripad) | 1957 |
| Goa liberated (Operation Vijay) — Goa becomes part of the Indian Union | 1961 |

**The story:** the order to remember is **Air India (1953) → SBI (1955) → Kerala Communist govt (1957) → Goa (1961)**. Separately, the **Hind Mazdoor Sabha (HMS)**, a socialist trade union, was founded in **1948** by **Ashok Mehta, T.S. Ramanujam and G.G. Mehta**.

**Andhra Pradesh & the foreign enclaves:**

- **Andhra Pradesh (1 Nov 1956)** merged Andhra State with the Telugu districts of Hyderabad State under the **Gentlemen's Agreement (1956)**, which balanced Andhra and Telangana interests.
- **Puducherry:** the French enclaves (Pondicherry, Karaikal, Mahe, Yanam) were transferred **de facto in 1954** and the transfer was **ratified by treaty in 1962**.

**Later reorganisation & privy purses:**

- **Privy purses** were abolished in **1971** by the **26th Constitutional Amendment**.
- **Sikkim** became India's **22nd state in 1975** via the **36th Constitutional Amendment**.
- **Telangana** was formed on **2 June 2014** as the **29th state**, bifurcated from Andhra Pradesh.

**Terms explained**

- **Nationalised:** brought under government ownership from private hands.
- **Privy purse:** the yearly payment the Indian government promised to former princely rulers in return for their accession; abolished in 1971.
- **Gentlemen's Agreement (1956):** an informal pact giving assurances to the Telangana region before Andhra Pradesh was formed.
- **Enclave:** a small foreign-held territory surrounded by Indian land (here, the French possessions).

**Don't confuse:** **Operation Vijay = Goa (1961)**, not Hyderabad (that was Operation Polo, 1948). **Privy purses = 26th Amendment (1971)**; **Sikkim = 36th Amendment (1975)**.

**Remember it:** milestone order 'A-S-K-G' = **Air India 1953, SBI 1955, Kerala 1957, Goa 1961**.

**TL;DR**

- Chronology: Air India nationalised 1953 → Imperial Bank became SBI 1955 → Kerala's Communist govt (EMS) 1957 → Goa liberated 1961.
- Hind Mazdoor Sabha (1948) founded by Ashok Mehta, T.S. Ramanujam and G.G. Mehta.
- Andhra Pradesh (1 Nov 1956) formed under the Gentlemen's Agreement (1956); Puducherry transferred by France (de facto 1954, treaty 1962).
- Privy purses abolished in 1971 by the 26th Constitutional Amendment.
- Sikkim = 22nd state (1975, 36th Amendment); Telangana = 29th state (2 June 2014).
keyPoints: Chronology: Air India nationalised 1953 → Imperial Bank became SBI 1955 → Kerala's Communist govt (EMS) 1957 → Goa liberated 1961.
Hind Mazdoor Sabha (1948) founded by Ashok Mehta, T.S. Ramanujam and G.G. Mehta.
Andhra Pradesh (1 Nov 1956) formed under the Gentlemen's Agreement (1956); Puducherry transferred by France (de facto 1954, treaty 1962).
Privy purses abolished in 1971 by the 26th Constitutional Amendment.
Sikkim = 22nd state (1975, 36th Amendment); Telangana = 29th state (2 June 2014).
items.mnemonic: Milestone order 'A-S-K-G': Air India 1953, SBI 1955, Kerala 1957, Goa 1961.

items.title: How the Accessions of 1947 Were Won — Detail
items.body:
### How the Accessions of 1947 Were Won — Detail

**In one line**
A new department, one speech to the princes, and a few stubborn rulers — the first phase of integration.

**The story**
Patel's **States Department** opened on **5 July 1947** with V.P. Menon as secretary. On 25 July Mountbatten told the **Chamber of Princes** that accession was their safest course. Menon counted **562** states (most books say about 565). By 15 August 1947 every state within India's borders had signed **except Junagadh**, Hyderabad and Jammu & Kashmir. Several others wavered first. In Travancore the Dewan **C.P. Ramaswami Iyer** declared independence, but the state acceded in July after an attack on him. In Jodhpur, Maharaja **Hanwant Singh** courted Jinnah before signing. In Bhopal, Nawab **Hamidullah Khan** held out until Delhi took the state over in 1949. Mysore's **Jayachamarajendra Wadiyar** acceded and later served as Rajpramukh. In the Andhra country the small state of **Banganapalle** merged into Madras in 1948, as **Pudukkottai** did in the Tamil country.

#### First-phase accessions

| State / step | Fact |
|---|---|
| **States Department** | **5 July 1947** — Patel (minister), V.P. Menon (secretary) |
| **25 July 1947** | Mountbatten's address to the **Chamber of Princes** |
| **How many states** | **562** (V.P. Menon) / ~565 (textbooks) |
| **By 15 Aug 1947** | All had acceded **except Junagadh**, Hyderabad and J&K |
| **Travancore** | Dewan **C.P. Ramaswami Iyer** declared independence; acceded July 1947 |
| **Jodhpur** | Maharaja **Hanwant Singh** courted Jinnah; acceded Aug 1947 |
| **Bhopal** | Nawab **Hamidullah Khan**; Chief Commissioner's province 1 June 1949 |
| **Banganapalle** (AP) | Merged into Madras Province, Feb 1948 (now Nandyal district) |
| **Pudukkottai** | Merged into Madras, March 1948 |
| **Mysore** | Acceded Aug 1947; Maharaja **Jayachamarajendra Wadiyar** Rajpramukh 1950–56 |

**Don't confuse**
- **562** = V.P. Menon's count; **565** = the round textbook figure; both refer to the same states.
- **Travancore** (C.P. Ramaswami Iyer) and **Jodhpur** (Hanwant Singh) wavered but acceded in 1947 — they are NOT among the three hard cases.

**TL;DR**
- States Department 5 July 1947; Chamber of Princes address 25 July 1947; 562 states (Menon).
- All but Junagadh, Hyderabad and J&K acceded by 15 Aug 1947.
- Waverers: Travancore (C.P. Ramaswami Iyer), Jodhpur (Hanwant Singh), Bhopal (Hamidullah Khan).
- Banganapalle (AP) and Pudukkottai merged into Madras in 1948.
keyPoints: The States Department was created on 5 July 1947.
By 15 August 1947 all states except Junagadh, Hyderabad and Jammu & Kashmir had acceded.
Travancore's Dewan C.P. Ramaswami Iyer declared independence before the state acceded.
Banganapalle in the Andhra region merged into Madras Province in 1948.

items.title: Junagadh, Hyderabad and Kashmir — Detail
items.body:
### Junagadh, Hyderabad and Kashmir — Detail

**In one line**
The names and dates behind the three states that did not accede by 15 August 1947.

**The story**
**Junagadh.** The Nawab **Mahabat Khan** III, advised by his Dewan **Shah Nawaz Bhutto**, announced accession to Pakistan. Most of his subjects were Hindu. Samaldas Gandhi formed a government-in-exile, the **Arzi Hukumat**. India took over on **9 November 1947**, and the plebiscite of **20 February 1948** confirmed the choice for India.

**Hyderabad.** Nizam **Mir Osman Ali Khan** signed a Standstill Agreement on **29 November 1947**. K.M. Munshi went to Hyderabad as India's **Agent-General**, while Mir **Laik Ali** was the Nizam's Prime Minister. The Razakars of the **Ittehad**ul Muslimeen spread terror. Operation Polo (**13**–**17 September 1948**) ended the standoff. Maj-Gen **J.N. Chaudhuri** became Military Governor, and the civil servant **Vellodi** became Chief Minister in 1950. The Nizam stayed on as **Rajpramukh of Hyderabad**. 17 September is remembered as Hyderabad **Liberation Day**.

**Kashmir.** Tribal raiders invaded on **22 October 1947**. Hari Singh acceded on 26 October, and on **27 October 1947** Mountbatten accepted and Indian troops landed at Srinagar. India went to the UN on **1 January 1948**, and the ceasefire came on **1 January 1949**. **Sheikh Abdullah** led the administration. Article 370 was made inoperative on **5 August 2019**, and two UTs followed on **31 October 2019**.

#### The hard cases

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Junagadh — ruler** | Nawab **Mahabat Khan** III; acceded to Pakistan, 15 Aug 1947 |
| **Junagadh — Dewan** | **Shah Nawaz Bhutto** (father of Z.A. Bhutto) |
| **Arzi Hukumat** | Junagadh government-in-exile — **Samaldas Gandhi**, Sept 1947 |
| **Junagadh — outcome** | Taken over **9 November 1947**; plebiscite **20 February 1948** |
| **Hyderabad — ruler** | Nizam **Mir Osman Ali Khan** (VII) |
| **Hyderabad — standstill** | Signed **29 November 1947** (one year) |
| **India in Hyderabad** | K.M. Munshi, **Agent-General** (1948) |
| **Nizam's PM** | Mir **Laik Ali** |
| **Razakars** | Militia of the Majlis-e-**Ittehad**ul Muslimeen (Kasim Razvi) |
| **Operation Polo** | **13**–**17 September 1948** (Police Action) |
| **After Polo** | Maj-Gen **J.N. Chaudhuri**, Military Governor |
| **Civil rule** | M.K. **Vellodi**, Chief Minister 1950 |
| **Nizam after 1948** | **Rajpramukh of Hyderabad** 1950–56 |
| **17 September** | Hyderabad **Liberation Day** |
| **Kashmir — raid** | Tribal invasion, **22 October 1947** |
| **Kashmir — response** | Accession accepted & troops airlifted, **27 October 1947** |
| **UN reference** | **1 January 1948** |
| **Ceasefire** | **1 January 1949** |
| **Sheikh Abdullah** | Emergency administration 1947; J&K Prime Minister 1948 |
| **2019** | 370 inoperative **5 August 2019**; two UTs from **31 October 2019** |

**Don't confuse**
- **Junagadh** = plebiscite (20 Feb 1948); **Hyderabad** = Operation Polo (13–17 Sept 1948); **Kashmir** = accession under invasion (26–27 Oct 1947).
- **Operation Polo** ≠ **Operation Vijay** (Goa, 1961) ≠ **Operation Gulmarg** (the Pakistani code name for the 1947 tribal raid).

**TL;DR**
- Junagadh: Mahabat Khan III, Dewan Shah Nawaz Bhutto, Arzi Hukumat (Samaldas Gandhi), takeover 9 Nov 1947, plebiscite 20 Feb 1948.
- Hyderabad: Mir Osman Ali Khan; standstill 29 Nov 1947; Munshi Agent-General; Polo 13–17 Sept 1948; J.N. Chaudhuri; Nizam Rajpramukh.
- Kashmir: raid 22 Oct 1947; troops 27 Oct; UN 1 Jan 1948; ceasefire 1 Jan 1949; Sheikh Abdullah.
- Article 370 inoperative 5 Aug 2019; UTs J&K and Ladakh 31 Oct 2019.
keyPoints: The Junagadh plebiscite was held on 20 February 1948.
Operation Polo lasted from 13 to 17 September 1948.
K.M. Munshi was India's Agent-General in Hyderabad.
India referred the Kashmir issue to the UN on 1 January 1948.

items.title: The Second Phase — Mergers, Unions and Privy Purses
items.body:
### The Second Phase — Mergers, Unions and Privy Purses

**In one line**
Accession only gave the Centre three subjects; in 1948–50 Patel and Menon dissolved the states themselves into provinces and unions.

**The story**
Small states went into the provinces next door. The **Orissa** states merged first, on **1 January 1948**, and the Chhattisgarh states joined the **Central Provinces** the same day. **Baroda** went into Bombay, and **Cooch Behar** into **West Bengal**. Larger clusters became **unions of states**, each under a Rajpramukh. **Saurashtra** was first, on **15 February 1948**; then came **Matsya**, **Vindhya Pradesh**, **Madhya Bharat** and **PEPSU** (**Patiala**). Rajasthan grew in stages to Greater Rajasthan (**30 March 1949**), and **Travancore-Cochin** was united on **1 July 1949**. Some areas were run directly from Delhi. Himachal Pradesh (**15 April 1948**) was formed from the hill states, and **Bilaspur** joined it in **1954**. In the north-east, **Bodhachandra** Singh signed Manipur's merger on **21 September 1949**, and Tripura followed under **Kanchan Prabha Devi**. The rulers kept titles and privy purses, guaranteed by Articles **291** and **362**. When Indira Gandhi derecognised them, the **Madhav Rao Scindia** case (1970) went against the government; the 26th Amendment (1971) ended the purses. The 7th Amendment (1956) had already **abolished the office of Rajpramukh**.

#### Mergers and unions

| Unit | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Orissa states** | Merged into **Orissa**, **1 January 1948** (first) |
| **Chhattisgarh states** | Merged into the **Central Provinces**, 1 Jan 1948 |
| **Saurashtra** | First union of states, **15 February 1948** (Kathiawar) |
| **Matsya Union** | Alwar, Bharatpur, Dholpur, Karauli — March 1948 |
| **Vindhya Pradesh** | Bundelkhand & Baghelkhand states, April 1948 (Rewa) |
| **Madhya Bharat** | Gwalior, Indore & Malwa states, May 1948 |
| **PEPSU** | **Patiala** and East Punjab States Union, 15 July 1948 |
| **Rajasthan** | Built in stages; Greater Rajasthan **30 March 1949** |
| **Travancore-Cochin** | United **1 July 1949** |
| **Himachal Pradesh** | ~30 hill states, **15 April 1948** (Chief Commissioner's province) |
| **Baroda** | Merged into Bombay, 1 May 1949 |
| **Cooch Behar** | Part of **West Bengal** from 1 Jan 1950 |
| **Manipur** | Maharaja **Bodhachandra** Singh, Shillong, **21 September 1949** (effective 15 Oct) |
| **Tripura** | Merged 15 Oct 1949 — Regent **Kanchan Prabha Devi** |
| **Bilaspur** | Part C state 1950 → into Himachal Pradesh **1954** |
| **Privy purse — guarantee** | Articles **291** & **362** |
| **Privy Purse case** | **Madhav Rao Scindia** v. Union of India (1970) → 26th Amendment (1971) |
| **End of Rajpramukhs** | 7th Amendment (1956) **abolished the office of Rajpramukh** |

**Don't confuse**
- **Saurashtra** (Feb 1948) = first **union** of states; **Orissa states** (1 Jan 1948) = first **merger** into a province.
- **PEPSU** = Patiala and East Punjab States Union — a Part B state, not a part of British Punjab.

**TL;DR**
- Mergers: Orissa & Chhattisgarh states 1 Jan 1948; Baroda 1949; Cooch Behar → West Bengal 1950.
- Unions: Saurashtra 15 Feb 1948 (first), Matsya, Vindhya Pradesh, Madhya Bharat, PEPSU, Rajasthan (30 Mar 1949), Travancore-Cochin (1 July 1949).
- Centre-run: Himachal Pradesh 15 Apr 1948; Bilaspur → HP 1954; Manipur (Bodhachandra, 21 Sept 1949) and Tripura (Oct 1949).
- Privy purses: Arts 291 & 362 → Madhav Rao Scindia case 1970 → 26th Amendment 1971; Rajpramukh ended 1956.

PEPSU stands for Patiala and East Punjab States Union.
Manipur Merger Agreement was signed on 21 September 1949.
Privy purses were guaranteed by Articles 291 and 362.

items.title: French and Portuguese Enclaves, and Sikkim
items.body:
### French and Portuguese Enclaves, and Sikkim

**In one line**
After the princes came the foreign pockets — France left by negotiation, Portugal had to be forced out — and finally Sikkim joined as a state.

**The story**
France negotiated its exit. **Chandernagore** voted to join India in 1949 and became part of West Bengal in 1954. The **Kizhoor** referendum (1954) brought the de facto transfer of Pondicherry, Karaikal, Mahe and **Yanam** on 1 November 1954. Yanam is an ex-French pocket inside Andhra Pradesh, near Kakinada. The de jure transfer came in 1962, and the **14th Amendment** made Pondicherry a UT. Portugal refused to leave. Volunteers freed **Dadra** and Nagar Haveli in 1954, and the **10th Amendment** (1961) made it a UT. Goa, Daman and Diu were taken in Operation Vijay; **19 December** is Goa Liberation Day. The **12th Amendment** (1962) made them a UT. In the **Opinion Poll** of 1967 Goans refused to merge with Maharashtra, and Goa became a state on **30 May 1987** (**56th** Amendment). The two western UTs merged on **26 January 2020**. Sikkim, an Indian protectorate since 1950, became an '**associate state**' by the **35th Amendment** (1974). After a referendum removed the **Chogyal**, it became the 22nd state on **16 May 1975**, with **Kazi Lhendup Dorji** as Chief Minister.

#### Enclaves and Sikkim

| Territory / step | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Chandernagore** (French) | Referendum 1949 → de facto 1950 → into West Bengal 1954 |
| **Kizhoor referendum** | 18 Oct 1954 → de facto transfer of the French settlements, 1 Nov 1954 |
| **Pondicherry UT** | **14th Amendment** (1962); de jure transfer 16 Aug 1962 |
| **Yanam** (AP angle) | Ex-French; enclave inside AP (Kakinada area); part of Puducherry UT |
| **Operation Vijay** | 18–**19 December** 1961 — Goa Liberation Day |
| **Goa UT** | **12th Amendment** (1962) — Goa, Daman & Diu |
| **Goa Opinion Poll** | 16 Jan 1967 — rejected merger with Maharashtra |
| **Goa statehood** | **30 May 1987** — **56th** Amendment; 25th state |
| **Dadra & Nagar Haveli** | Freed by volunteers 1954; UT by **10th Amendment** (1961) |
| **Merged UT** | DNH + Daman & Diu, **26 January 2020** |
| **Sikkim 1974** | **35th Amendment** — "**associate state**" |
| **Sikkim 1975** | Referendum ended the **Chogyal** monarchy; 22nd state **16 May 1975** |
| **Sikkim — first CM** | **Kazi Lhendup Dorji** |

**Don't confuse**
- **10th Amendment** = Dadra & Nagar Haveli; **12th** = Goa, Daman & Diu; **14th** = Pondicherry; **35th** = Sikkim associate state; **36th** = Sikkim full state; **56th** = Goa statehood.
- **Yanam** sits inside **Andhra Pradesh** but belongs to **Puducherry** UT.

**TL;DR**
- French: Chandernagore → West Bengal 1954; Kizhoor referendum → de facto 1 Nov 1954; 14th Amendment 1962 (UT).
- Yanam: ex-French, inside AP, part of Puducherry.
- Portuguese: Dadra & NH freed 1954, 10th Amendment 1961; Goa — Operation Vijay, 19 Dec Liberation Day, 12th Amendment 1962, Opinion Poll 1967, statehood 30 May 1987 (56th).
- Sikkim: 35th Amendment 1974 (associate state) → referendum → 22nd state 16 May 1975 (36th); CM Kazi Lhendup Dorji.
keyPoints: Pondicherry became a Union Territory by the 14th Amendment (1962).
Yanam, a former French settlement, lies inside Andhra Pradesh.
The 12th Amendment (1962) made Goa, Daman and Diu a Union Territory.
Sikkim became an associate state by the 35th Amendment (1974).

items.title: The Road to 1956 — Commissions and the Act in Detail
items.body:
### The Road to 1956 — Commissions and the Act in Detail

**In one line**
Who sat on the commissions, when they reported, and what the 1956 Act actually changed.

**The story**
The Constituent Assembly's President appointed the **Linguistic Provinces Commission** under **S.K. Dhar** in June 1948. It advised against linguistic states. The Congress then set up the JVP Committee at its **Jaipur** session (December 1948); it reported in **April 1949** and urged delay. Andhra's agitation changed the mood. The Fazl Ali SRC, appointed in December 1953, reported on **30 September 1955**. It judged boundaries by four tests: national unity, linguistic and cultural **homogeneity**, financial and administrative **viability**, and the welfare of the people. The States Reorganisation Act came into force on **1 November 1956**. It also created **five** **Zonal Councils** for inter-state cooperation. It formed Kerala from Travancore-Cochin and **Malabar**, and left Bombay a **bilingual** state — the seed of the 1960 split.

#### Commissions and the 1956 Act

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Dhar Commission** | **Linguistic Provinces Commission**, **S.K. Dhar**, June 1948 |
| **JVP Committee** | Set up at **Jaipur** Congress, Dec 1948; reported **April 1949** |
| **SRC timeline** | Appointed Dec 1953; report **30 September 1955** |
| **SRC criteria** | Unity & security; linguistic/cultural **homogeneity**; financial & administrative **viability**; welfare |
| **SRA in force** | **1 November 1956** |
| **Zonal Councils** | **five** — N, C, E, W, S (SRA 1956) |
| **Kerala (1956)** | Travancore-Cochin + **Malabar** |
| **Bombay (1956)** | Left a **bilingual** state — Marathi + Gujarati |

**Don't confuse**
- The **Dhar Commission** was appointed by the **Constituent Assembly President**; the **JVP Committee** by the **Congress**; the **SRC** by the **Government of India** (1953).
- **Zonal Councils** (five) were created by the **SRA 1956** — they are statutory, not constitutional.

**TL;DR**
- Dhar (Linguistic Provinces Commission) June 1948; JVP at Jaipur Congress, report April 1949.
- SRC: appointed Dec 1953, report 30 Sept 1955; four criteria (unity, homogeneity, viability, welfare).
- SRA in force 1 Nov 1956; five Zonal Councils.
- Kerala = Travancore-Cochin + Malabar; Bombay left bilingual.
keyPoints: The Dhar Commission was officially the Linguistic Provinces Commission.
The SRC submitted its report on 30 September 1955.
The States Reorganisation Act, 1956 created five Zonal Councils.
Kerala was formed in 1956 from Travancore-Cochin and Malabar.

items.title: New States after 1956 — Year, Act and Amendment
items.body:
### New States after 1956 — Year, Act and Amendment

**In one line**
The 1956 map kept changing: language in the west and Punjab, tribal identity in the north-east, development in 2000.

**The story**
Bombay split into Maharashtra and Gujarat on **1 May 1960**, after the Samyukta Maharashtra and Mahagujarat (**Indulal Yagnik**) movements. **Nagaland** followed on **1 December 1963**, with special status under Article **371A**. The **Punjabi Suba** campaign of Master Tara Singh and **Sant Fateh Singh** led to the **Shah Commission**, and Haryana was carved out on 1 November 1966. Himachal Pradesh became a state on **25 January 1971**. Meghalaya was first an **autonomous state** within Assam (**22nd Amendment**). It became a full state with Manipur and Tripura on **21 January 1972**. Mizoram (after the 1986 accord with **Laldenga**, **53rd** Amendment) and **Arunachal** (**55th**) became states on 20 February 1987. In 2000 came Chhattisgarh (1 Nov), Uttarakhand (**9 Nov**; first called **Uttaranchal**) and Jharkhand (**15 Nov**). Renamings followed: Madras to **Tamil Nadu** (1969) and Mysore to **Karnataka** (1973). Delhi became the National Capital Territory by the **69th Amendment** (1991).

#### After 1956

| State / change | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Maharashtra & Gujarat** | **1 May 1960** — Bombay Reorganisation Act |
| **Mahagujarat movement** | **Indulal Yagnik**; with the Samyukta Maharashtra movement |
| **Nagaland** | **1 December 1963**; 13th Amendment, Art **371A** |
| **Punjab–Haryana** | **Shah Commission** (1966); Haryana 1 Nov 1966 |
| **Punjabi Suba** | Master Tara Singh, **Sant Fateh Singh** |
| **Himachal statehood** | **25 January 1971** |
| **Meghalaya** | **Autonomous state** 1970 (**22nd Amendment**) → full state 1972 |
| **NE reorganisation** | Manipur, Tripura, Meghalaya — **21 January 1972** |
| **Mizoram** | Mizo Accord 1986 (**Laldenga**); state 20 Feb 1987, **53rd** Amendment |
| **Arunachal Pradesh** | State 20 Feb 1987, **55th** Amendment |
| **2000 trio** | Chhattisgarh 1 Nov, Uttarakhand **9 Nov**, Jharkhand **15 Nov** 2000 |
| **Uttarakhand** | Formed **9 Nov** 2000 as **Uttaranchal**; renamed 2007 |
| **Chhattisgarh** | From MP, 1 Nov 2000 — **26th** state |
| **Renamings** | Madras → **Tamil Nadu** (1969); Mysore → **Karnataka** (1973) |
| **Delhi** | National Capital Territory — **69th Amendment** (1991) |

**Don't confuse**
- **Nagaland (1963)** came before the 1972 north-east trio; **Mizoram & Arunachal (1987)** came last.
- The source PDF lists Himachal with Punjab/Haryana under 1966 (it gained the Punjab hill areas then as a UT); **statehood was 25 January 1971**.

**TL;DR**
- Maharashtra & Gujarat 1 May 1960; Nagaland 1 Dec 1963 (371A); Haryana 1 Nov 1966 (Shah Commission).
- HP state 25 Jan 1971; Manipur, Tripura, Meghalaya 21 Jan 1972 (Meghalaya autonomous 1970, 22nd Amendment).
- Mizoram (Laldenga, 53rd) & Arunachal (55th) 20 Feb 1987; Goa 30 May 1987.
- Chhattisgarh 1 Nov, Uttarakhand 9 Nov, Jharkhand 15 Nov 2000; Tamil Nadu 1969, Karnataka 1973; Delhi NCT 1991.
keyPoints: Nagaland became a state on 1 December 1963.
Himachal Pradesh became a full state on 25 January 1971.
Mizoram became a state after the Mizo Accord with Laldenga.
Jharkhand was formed on 15 November 2000.

items.title: The First Council of Ministers and the Partition Settlement
items.body:
### The First Council of Ministers and the Partition Settlement

**In one line**
Independent India's first team, as the source PDF lists it, plus the boundary award and the pact that followed Partition.

**The story**
Nehru's first ministry was deliberately broad, taking in Congressmen, a Sikh leader, a Hindu Mahasabha leader, a Dalit leader and non-Congress experts. Nehru kept **External Affairs**; Patel held Home, States and **Information and Broadcasting**. **Azad** took **Education**, **Shanmukham Chetty** **Finance**, **Baldev Singh** **Defence** and **John Mathai** **Railways**. **Jagjivan Ram** held **Labour**, **Amrit Kaur** **Health** and **Kidwai** **Communications**. C.H. **Bhabha** had **Commerce**, **Gadgil** **Works, Mines and Power**, and **Daulatram** **Food and Agriculture**. K.C. Neogy managed **Relief and Rehabilitation**, and **Mookerjee** **Industries and Supplies**; Gopalaswami Ayyangar sat **without portfolio**. Ambedkar held Law. **Rajagopalachari** followed Mountbatten as the only Indian **Governor-General** (1948–50). The border had been drawn by Sir Cyril **Radcliffe**, whose award came out on **17 August 1947**, two days after independence. The **Nehru–Liaquat** Pact of **1950** pledged both countries to protect their minorities.

#### First Council of Ministers

| Minister | Portfolio |
|---|---|
| Jawaharlal Nehru | PM; **External Affairs** & Commonwealth Relations; Scientific Research |
| Vallabhbhai Patel | Deputy PM; Home, States, **Information and Broadcasting** |
| Maulana **Azad** | **Education** |
| R.K. **Shanmukham Chetty** | **Finance** |
| Sardar **Baldev Singh** | **Defence** |
| **John Mathai** | **Railways** and Transport |
| **Jagjivan Ram** | **Labour** |
| Rajkumari **Amrit Kaur** | **Health** |
| Rafi Ahmed **Kidwai** | **Communications** |
| C.H. **Bhabha** | **Commerce** |
| N.V. **Gadgil** | **Works, Mines and Power** |
| Jairamdas **Daulatram** | **Food and Agriculture** |
| K.C. Neogy | **Relief and Rehabilitation** |
| Syama Prasad **Mookerjee** | **Industries and Supplies** (resigned April 1950) |
| N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar | Minister **without portfolio** |
| **Governor-General** | Mountbatten → **C. Rajagopalachari** (21 June 1948), the only Indian |
| **Radcliffe Line** | Sir Cyril **Radcliffe** — award published **17 August 1947** |
| **Nehru–Liaquat Pact** | Delhi, 8 April **1950** — protection of minorities |

**Don't confuse**
- **Shanmukham Chetty** was the first Finance Minister — **John Mathai** (Railways) succeeded him in Finance in 1948.
- The **Radcliffe Award** was published on **17 August 1947** — after independence day.

**TL;DR**
- Nehru External Affairs; Patel Home, States, I&B; Azad Education; Chetty Finance; Baldev Singh Defence.
- Jagjivan Ram Labour; Amrit Kaur Health; Kidwai Communications; Mookerjee Industries; Neogy Relief & Rehabilitation.
- Rajagopalachari — only Indian Governor-General (from 21 June 1948).
- Radcliffe Award 17 Aug 1947; Nehru–Liaquat Pact 8 April 1950 (minorities).
keyPoints: R.K. Shanmukham Chetty was the first Finance Minister of independent India.
Rajkumari Amrit Kaur was the first Health Minister.
C. Rajagopalachari was the only Indian Governor-General.
The Radcliffe Award was published on 17 August 1947.

items.title: For Mains — Post-Independence Consolidation & States Reorganisation
items.body:
This topic feeds **Mains Paper-II** (clause M2-5: 'Nationalism phases; peasant/women/tribal/workers movements; Independence & Partition; linguistic reorganisation'). Mains wants you to **argue a thesis** — for example, that integration and linguistic reorganisation together turned a fragmented inheritance into a stable, democratic federation — rather than list dates.

**Dimensions Mains asks**

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| The challenge | 565 states + Partition refugees + a patchwork of provinces threatened 'balkanisation' |
| Methods of integration | Persuasion + privy purses + Instrument of Accession; plebiscite (Junagadh), force (Hyderabad), diplomacy (Kashmir) |
| Linguistic reorganisation | Fear vs aspiration; Dhar/JVP caution; Andhra breakthrough; Fazl Ali's balanced formula |
| Significance | Territorial unity without large-scale coercion; federalism strengthened, not weakened |
| Criticism/limits | Hyderabad 'Police Action' violence; Article 370 tensions; later sub-regional demands (Telangana) |
| Way forward | Cooperative federalism; linguistic–administrative balance in future state demands |

**Data points / reports to quote:** 565 princely states; Instrument of Accession (3 subjects); Operation Polo (Sept 1948); Potti Sreeramulu's death (15 Dec 1952); Andhra State (1 Oct 1953, first linguistic state); Fazl Ali Commission (16 states + 3 UTs recommended); States Reorganisation Act 1956 (14 states, 6 UTs; 7th Amendment); privy purses abolished (26th Amendment, 1971).

**AP angle:** Andhra is the pivot of the whole linguistic-reorganisation story — **Potti Sreeramulu's sacrifice** made Andhra State the first linguistic state, and the **Gentlemen's Agreement (1956)** behind Andhra Pradesh foreshadowed the later Telangana movement, letting you connect 1953, 1956 and 2014 in one arc.

**Use in answers:** open with the 'two simultaneous nation-building tasks' (integration + reorganisation); use Andhra as the case study bridging both; close by arguing that linguistic states strengthened unity (counter the 1950s fear). A timeline diagram (1947 integration → 1953 Andhra → 1956 SRA → 2014 Telangana) adds value.
keyPoints: Serves Mains Paper-II clause M2-5 (Independence & Partition; linguistic reorganisation).
Thesis: integration + linguistic reorganisation built a stable democratic federation from a fragmented inheritance.
Quote: 565 states, Operation Polo (1948), Andhra State (1 Oct 1953), SRA 1956 (14 states/6 UTs, 7th Amendment).
Criticism: Hyderabad Police Action violence, Article 370 tension, later Telangana demand.
AP angle: Potti Sreeramulu + Gentlemen's Agreement 1956 link 1953 → 1956 → 2014.
